seoTitle: Shipping Container Homes India │ Custom-Built │ SAMAN
metaDescription: Shipping container homes with a reinforced MS shell from Rs 3.64 lakh ex-GST. Built for relocation and coastal duty, six sizes, factory-made, pan-India delivery.
opener: Shipping container homes from SAMAN are the reinforced build in our range: heavier 75x75 mm corner posts, a full-height 1.6 mm corrugated MS shell, continuous ridge sealing and zinc-rich primer under the enamel, engineered for relocation and hard weather rather than a single quiet plot. These are newly fabricated container-form homes made in our Bengaluru and Greater Noida works; we do not resell used cargo boxes, and a converted ISO container is only ever a separately quoted option. Prices run from Rs 3,64,320 ex-GST at 20x8 ft to Rs 9,13,920 at 40x12 ft across six sizes.
descriptionHtml:
What "shipping container home" means here, and what it does not

The name describes a shape and a standard, not a source.

A shipping container home from SAMAN is newly fabricated to container dimensions and container hardware standards. It has the proportions, the corner-casting geometry and the handling points of a shipping container because those things are genuinely useful in a building that will be lifted, transported and set down more than once. What it does not have is a history at sea. No unit on this page began life carrying cargo. If you specifically want a used ISO container rebuilt and supplied as new, we do that, and it is quoted separately on request.

That distinction matters commercially, not just semantically. A used cargo hull comes with a service history you cannot see: cargo residues, floor treatments, repairs of unknown quality, and corrosion that starts from the inside. Rebuilding one honestly costs more than fabricating new to the same dimensions, which is why the conversion route is a specific request rather than the default.

Prices run from ₹3,64,320 ex-GST at 20 × 8 ft to ₹9,13,920 at 40 × 12 ft.

What is actually reinforced, and why

This is the heavy build in the range, and the specification differs from the standard container house in four measurable ways.

Corner posts are 75 × 75 mm rather than the standard section. Corners are where a lifted building is loaded, and a unit that will be craned repeatedly takes that load through the same four points every time.

The shell is 1.6 mm full height, against 1.2 mm standard. That is a stiffness decision as much as a durability one — a thicker skin resists the racking that comes from lifting an asymmetrically loaded building, and racking is what opens joints.

Ridge sealing is continuous rather than lapped. A roof that has been lifted, transported over a rough road and set down is a roof whose joints have been worked. A continuous seal has nothing to work loose.

Zinc-rich primer sits under the enamel. This is the coastal specification. Standard red-oxide primer is entirely adequate inland; within a few kilometres of saltwater it is not, and a zinc-rich system is the difference between a coating that lasts a decade and one that fails in three years.

Everything else follows the range specification: welded MS chassis, 75 mm mineral wool in the walls, 100 mm glasswool over the ceiling, 8 mm pre-laminated internal lining, cement-fibre floor deck with a resilient finish, concealed copper circuits with distribution board, MCBs, RCCB and earth.

Six sizes, and how reinforcement changes each

20 × 8 ft — 160 sq ft. The size most often relocated, and the one where the reinforcement pays back fastest. A 160 square foot unit is light enough to be lifted by modest equipment, which in practice means it gets moved more casually and more often than larger units. The heavier corner posts exist for exactly that treatment.

20 × 10 ft — 200 sq ft. Common on project sites where the same accommodation follows the work from one location to the next over several years. At this size and weight the difference between a standard shell and a 1.6 mm one shows up after the third move rather than the first.

20 × 12 ft — 240 sq ft. Wider than standard container proportions, which means transport needs checking rather than assuming. The reinforcement matters here for a different reason: a wider building has a longer unsupported span across the roof, and a stiffer shell keeps that span honest under handling loads.

40 × 8 ft — 320 sq ft. The classic relocatable form. Forty feet of length on eight feet of width is the geometry the entire container standard was built around, so this size travels more easily than any other in the range and needs no escort on standard roads.

40 × 10 ft — 400 sq ft. A family-sized home that can still be moved. This is the size most often bought by people who expect to relocate once — a plot they may leave, a lease that may not renew — rather than by those who move routinely.

40 × 12 ft — 480 sq ft. The largest, and the one where relocation stops being casual. At this width transport requires planning and often escort. The reinforcement here is less about frequent handling and more about the two or three significant moves the unit will make across its life.

Coastal and industrial exposure

Half of what makes this build different is invisible, and it is the coating.

Steel near saltwater fails from the coating inward. Chlorides carried in humid air settle on the surface, penetrate any break in the enamel, and begin working on the steel beneath while the paint above still looks intact. By the time corrosion is visible from outside, it has been running for some time.

Zinc-rich primer changes the chemistry of that process. It sacrifices itself in preference to the steel, so a break in the enamel becomes a slow problem rather than a fast one. It is the standard specification for marine and industrial structures and it is why this build exists as a separate product rather than as an option box.

If your site is within a few kilometres of the coast, in an industrial zone with airborne chemicals, or somewhere with genuinely aggressive humidity, this is the build to choose regardless of whether you intend to move the unit. Tell us the location and the exposure at enquiry — the coating system is specified against the site, not against the product name.

Where this sits against the rest of the range

The five container-house builds each optimise for something different, and the reinforcement on this page is a durability and handling decision rather than a comfort one.

If the building will stand on one plot for its whole life and what matters is how it feels inside, the villa-grade interior specification puts the money where you will notice it — acoustic insulation, coffered ceilings, engineered wood and feature glazing — on the same structure. If you need the same home several times over, identical factory modules with a fixed drawing and sealed connection details is the economic route for colony and multi-unit work. If the budget is fixed, the lowest per-square-foot rate we publish achieves it by fixing one plan per size rather than by thinning the construction.

If you want a unit that arrives finished and needs no site team at all, that is quoted against your drawing.

The shared construction detail and the standard price ladder are on our container house range.

What the price includes, and what it does not

Ex-factory and ex-GST, ₹3,64,320 to ₹9,13,920 across six sizes.

That covers the complete building with the reinforced specification: heavier corner posts, 1.6 mm shell, continuous ridge sealing, zinc-rich primer under enamel, plus the full standard envelope, internal lining, flooring, electrical installation, bathroom, doors and windows and factory finishing.

It does not cover the plinth, the connection from your supply, transport or craneage.

Two things specific to this build are worth knowing before you compare it on price. First, the reinforcement is not an upgrade you can add later — corner posts and shell gauge are fabrication decisions, so a standard unit cannot be converted afterwards. Second, if the unit will be relocated, budget for the moves. Craneage and transport at each end are the recurring cost of a relocatable building, and they are usually larger than buyers expect on the second and third moves.

Delivery, relocation and installation

Seven to twenty-one working days from confirmed drawing.

Your site needs a level, cured plinth sized to the unit, trailer and crane access with the turning radius measured, and services brought to the connection side. That is the same as every build in the range.

What is specific here is what happens at the second location. Every unit carries designed lifting points, and those points are the only ones that should be used — a building lifted from anywhere else is a building whose warranty conversation becomes difficult. Before a relocation, the sensible sequence is to disconnect services properly, check the coating at the corner castings, and confirm the receiving plinth is level before the unit arrives rather than after.

Delivery is free inside Bengaluru city and across Delhi NCR including Ghaziabad, Gurugram, Faridabad, Noida and Greater Noida. Elsewhere freight is charged by distance and trailer size, confirmed with the quotation.

Transport, permits and what to check on arrival

A relocatable building is only as relocatable as the route to it, and this is the part buyers most often leave until last.

Standard container dimensions travel on ordinary trailers on ordinary roads. The 20 × 8 ft and 40 × 8 ft units are the easiest, because eight feet of width is inside every normal limit. At ten feet the movement is still routine but the turning radius at your gate becomes the constraint rather than the road. At twelve feet you are into over-dimensional territory in most states, which means route planning, sometimes escort, and a delivery window governed by permitted hours rather than by convenience.

None of that is difficult, but all of it is easier to arrange three weeks out than three days out. Tell us the delivery address at enquiry rather than at order, and the freight band and any escort requirement come back with the quotation instead of appearing afterwards.

When the unit arrives, there is a short list worth walking before the crane leaves. Check the four corner castings for transport damage, because that is where a knock will have landed. Check the ridge seal along its full length. Open and close every door and window, since racking in transit shows up in an opening that binds before it shows up anywhere else. Confirm the unit is sitting level on the plinth at all four corners rather than bridging. And photograph the coating at the corners before anything is connected, so that the condition on arrival is recorded rather than remembered.

That inspection takes fifteen minutes and it is the single most useful quarter hour in the whole process. A problem identified while the crane is still on site is an adjustment. The same problem found a week later is a return visit.

Warranty, service life and maintenance

5-year structural warranty and 1-year finishing warranty as standard; finishing warranty extendable to 2 years on request, confirmed at quotation.

Service life under proper use and maintenance is 20 to 25 years — an engineering expectation, not a warranty period.

Maintenance on a reinforced build is the standard coating schedule with one addition: inspect the corner castings and lifting points after every relocation. They are the parts that take the load and the parts most likely to have been knocked. A visual check and a touch-up of the coating at those four points, after each move, is most of what determines whether this unit reaches the top of its service-life range or the bottom.

We manufacture rather than resell. SAMAN POS India Private Limited has been building since 2009, incorporated in 2019, over 15 years of work, more than 500 projects delivered, and our own facilities in Bengaluru and Greater Noida.

Questions buyers ask about the reinforced build

Is this made from a real shipping container?

No. It is newly fabricated to container dimensions and hardware standards at our own works. A converted used ISO container is available as a separately quoted option on request, and it is genuinely a different product with different economics.

How many times can it be relocated?

There is no fixed number, and anyone who gives you one is guessing. What determines it is how it is lifted, how the coating is maintained at the corners, and how level the receiving base is each time. Units lifted from their designed points onto prepared plinths outlast units that are not, by a very wide margin.

Do I need this build if I am near the sea but never moving it?

Yes, and that is the more common reason to choose it. The zinc-rich primer is the coastal specification and it matters whether or not the building ever leaves the plot.

Can the reinforcement be added to a standard unit later?

No. Corner post section and shell gauge are set at fabrication. This has to be decided before the unit is built.

Is it heavier to transport?

Slightly, and it is accounted for in the freight band rather than surprising you at delivery. The heavier shell adds weight but stays within the same trailer class at every size.
